subject: Medicine
summary: A lumbar puncture (LP) is the gold standard for diagnosing meningitis and other central nervous system disorders. In resource‑limited hospitals, clinical judgment, basic CSF analysis, and rapid bedside tests guide management when advanced labs are unavailable.

sections.p: A lumbar puncture is the insertion of a needle into the lumbar subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for analysis. Diagnosis is based on CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen tests when available.
b: Technique: patient in lateral decubitus or sitting, lumbar region 1–2 vertebrae above the iliac crest, sterile field, local anaesthetic, 22‑25G needle

t.b: Measures intracranial pressure; >200 mmH2O suggests increased ICP, <80 mmH2O suggests low ICP
Differentiates bacterial (neutrophil predominance, >1000 cells/µL) from viral (lymphocyte predominance, 50–500 cells/µL) meningitis
Elevated in bacterial, TB, fungal meningitis; normal in viral
Low (<40 mg/dL or <2/3 serum) in bacterial/TB; normal in viral
Detects bacteria; positive in ~50% of bacterial meningitis
Positive in cryptococcal meningitis; useful when culture is delayed

sections.p: Severity is gauged by clinical features and CSF findings. In bacterial meningitis, rapid deterioration can occur; early recognition is critical.
b: Mild: fever, headache, no focal signs

sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa, the leading causes of meningitis are bacterial (especially *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Neisseria meningitidis*), tuberculous, and viral (enteroviruses).
b: Post‑vaccination meningitis – pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b

sections.p: Classic triad: fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status. In children, irritability, bulging fontanelle, vomiting. In TB, chronic headache, weight loss, night sweats.
b: Fever, headache, confusion

sections.p: Basic CSF analysis is essential. When advanced tests are unavailable, rely on Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen tests. Blood cultures and CRP guide systemic infection.
b: Microscopy of CSF – for parasites in endemic areas

sections.p: Contraindications include raised ICP (signs: papilledema, focal deficits), coagulopathy, local infection, and severe thrombocytopenia. Complications: post‑LP headache, bleeding, infection, herniation.
b: Post‑LP headache – advise lying flat, hydration

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause promptly. Empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis, antitubercular therapy for TB, antifungals for cryptococcal. Supportive care includes fluids, seizure control, and monitoring ICP.
b: Monitor vitals, glucose, electrolytes, and repeat CSF if clinical decline

sections.p: Repeat CSF when clinically indicated. Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib, and influenza reduces incidence. Counsel on HIV prevention and TB screening.
b: Educate on hand hygiene and avoiding crowded settings

sections.p: Meningitis can mimic viral encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and metabolic encephalopathy. CSF findings help differentiate.
b: Metabolic encephalopathy – normal CSF

sections.p: Low CSF glucose can be seen in TB and fungal meningitis; normal glucose does not exclude bacterial meningitis in neonates. Protein may be normal early in viral meningitis.
b: TB meningitis – CSF glucose may be low but not <20 mg/dL

whenToSeekHelp: Severe headache with vomiting and papilledema

faq.q: When is a lumbar puncture contraindicated?
faq.a: When there is suspected raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, focal deficits), coagulopathy, local infection, or severe thrombocytopenia.

faq.q: What is the first step if bacterial meningitis is suspected?
faq.a: Start empirical antibiotics immediately, then perform a lumbar puncture if the patient is stable and no contraindications.

faq.q: Why is dexamethasone added to treatment?
faq.a: It reduces inflammatory damage and improves outcomes in bacterial meningitis, especially with pneumococcus.

exam: What is the most urgent step in a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis and a normal CT? — Start empirical antibiotics before LP; then perform LP if no contraindications.
Which CSF finding differentiates bacterial from viral meningitis? — Neutrophil predominance and high opening pressure in bacterial; lymphocyte predominance and normal pressure in viral.
Why is a lumbar puncture avoided in a patient with papilledema? — Papilledema indicates raised ICP; LP could precipitate herniation.
What is the rationale for adding dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis? — It reduces inflammatory response and lowers mortality.
How would you manage a patient with suspected tuberculous meningitis in a setting without PCR? — Start RIPE therapy empirically and obtain CSF for culture and acid-fast stain; treat for 6–12 months.
Which rapid test is most useful for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV patients? — Cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay; positive result confirms diagnosis.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic exam identify meningitis, differentiate it from other CNS emergencies and reveal contraindications to lumbar puncture.
b: Onset and progression of fever (hours vs days).
Presence of neck stiffness, photophobia, headache, vomiting.
Altered mental status: irritability, lethargy, seizures, bulging fontanelle in infants.
Recent exposure to meningitis outbreaks, vaccination status, HIV or TB contacts.
Ear, sinus or dental infection, recent head trauma, neurosurgery.
Anticoagulant use, known coagulopathy, platelet count <50 000/µL, recent lumbar puncture or epidural.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: papilledema, focal neuro deficit, seizures, coma.

t.b: Elicited by extending the hip with knee flexed; pain or resistance = positive. Indicates meningeal irritation but may be absent in infants or early disease.
Passive neck flexion causing involuntary hip/knee flexion; positive suggests meningeal irritation. Not reliable in young children.
Palpate anterior fontanelle for bulging or tense tension; bulging = raised ICP, may contraindicate immediate LP.
Look for papilledema; presence = raised ICP, LP deferred until imaging clears.
Assess cranial nerves, motor strength, reflexes, gait. Focal deficits raise concern for mass lesion; obtain CT before LP.
Identify local infection over lumbar area; cellulitis or abscess contraindicates LP at that site.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: CSF analysis is the cornerstone; each test answers a specific diagnostic question. In low‑resource settings, prioritize Gram stain, culture, and rapid antigen tests.
b: CSF opening pressure – distinguishes normal, raised, or low pressure states.
Cell count and differential – neutrophils suggest bacterial, lymphocytes suggest viral, TB or fungal.
Protein – >45 mg/dL abnormal; >100 mg/dL strongly suggests bacterial or TB meningitis.
Glucose – CSF/serum ratio <0.4 or absolute <40 mg/dL points to bacterial, TB, or fungal infection.
Gram stain – rapid identification of bacteria; positive in ~60 % of bacterial meningitis.
Culture – definitive organism identification; incubate 48‑72 h, longer for TB.
Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) lateral flow assay – rapid detection in HIV patients; positive = cryptococcal meningitis.
Acid‑fast stain (Ziehl‑Neelsen) – look for Mycobacterium tuberculosis when TB suspected.

t.b: Answers: Is CSF pressure normal? Normal range in children 10‑20 cm H₂O. >25 cm H₂O = raised pressure; <5 cm H₂O = low pressure. If unavailable, infer from clinical signs.
Answers: Is glucose low? Calculate CSF/serum ratio. Ratio <0.4 or absolute <40 mg/dL suggests bacterial/TB/fungal. If serum glucose unavailable, use absolute cut‑off.
Answers: Is protein elevated? >45 mg/dL abnormal; >100 mg/dL favors bacterial/TB. In malnutrition protein may be lower; interpret with clinical picture.
Answers: Predominant cell type? >1000 cells/µL neutrophils = bacterial; <100 cells/µL lymphocytes = viral or TB. In HIV, mixed picture possible.
Answers: Is a bacterial organism seen? Positive = immediate targeted antibiotics. Negative does not exclude bacterial meningitis; proceed with culture.
Answers: Is cryptococcal antigen present? Positive = cryptococcal meningitis; start amphotericin‑based therapy. If unavailable, consider India‑ink microscopy.
Answers: Is TB bacilli seen? Positive confirms TB meningitis; start anti‑TB regimen. If unavailable, rely on lymphocytic CSF, low glucose, high protein.

sections.p: Classification combines clinical presentation with CSF parameters to guide urgency and level of care.
b: Bacterial meningitis – CSF neutrophils >1000/µL, protein >100 mg/dL, glucose ratio <0.4, positive Gram stain/culture.
Viral meningitis – CSF lymphocytes <100/µL, protein ≤100 mg/dL, glucose ratio ≥0.4, negative Gram stain.
TB meningitis – CSF lymphocytes predominance, protein >100 mg/dL, glucose ratio <0.4, acid‑fast stain or PCR positive.
Fungal meningitis – CSF lymphocytes, protein >100 mg/dL, glucose ratio <0.4, CrAg positive.
Severity grading (WHO/CDC) – Mild: fever, irritability, normal pressure; Moderate: altered mental status, seizures, pressure 20‑30 cm H₂O; Severe: coma, pressure >30 cm H₂O, focal deficits.

sections.p: Several acute neurologic illnesses mimic meningitis; bedside clues and targeted tests separate them.

t.b: Points: fever, altered mental status, focal seizures, normal CSF pressure, lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose. MRI or PCR for HSV if available.
Points: thunderclap headache, neck stiffness, xanthochromic CSF, RBC count >1000/µL that does not clear in tube 1 vs 2. CT first if within 6 h.
Points: altered consciousness without meningeal signs, normal CSF, abnormal electrolytes, glucose, renal/hepatic failure. Treat underlying metabolic derangement.

t.a: Acute bacterial sinusitis with orbital cellulitis
t.b: Points: localized facial pain, periorbital swelling, no meningeal signs, normal CSF. Imaging of sinuses clarifies.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures rapid control of infection, prevention of complications and safe monitoring, especially where resources are limited.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen and IV fluids if hypotensive.
2. Obtain blood cultures (at least two sets) before antibiotics, if this will not delay treatment.

3. Start empiric intravenous antibiotics covering the most likely pathogens for the age group and local epidemiology (e.g., third‑generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin for neonates and children; add ampicillin for Listeria in infants).
4. Give adjunctive dexamethasone intravenously before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce inflammatory damage in bacterial meningitis.
5. If TB meningitis is suspected and rapid PCR is unavailable, start empiric anti‑TB therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) plus adjunctive steroids.
6. Monitor vitals, mental status, urine output, and repeat CSF if clinical deterioration occurs or if initial CSF was inconclusive.
7. Escalate to intensive care for refractory shock, seizures, raised intracranial pressure, or need for mechanical ventilation; arrange neurosurgical review if signs of herniation develop.
8. Document and communicate results promptly; ensure completion of the full antibiotic course and arrange follow‑up for hearing assessment and neurodevelopmental screening.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse reactions and interactions allows timely mitigation without compromising antimicrobial efficacy.
b: Cephalosporins – can cause allergic rash, neutropenia, or renal tubular injury; stop if severe rash or rising creatinine, switch to carbapenem if needed.
Vancomycin – monitor for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; ensure trough levels are not excessively high, hydrate and consider alternative if creatinine rises.
Dexamethasone – may raise blood glucose; check capillary glucose in diabetics and treat hyperglycaemia; taper after 4 days to avoid adrenal suppression.
Rifampicin – induces hepatic enzymes, reducing concentrations of oral contraceptives and some antiretrovirals; counsel patients on alternative contraception and adjust ART if possible.

sections.p: Prompt identification of procedural and disease‑related complications prevents morbidity and mortality.
b: Post‑LP headache – treat with oral caffeine, hydration, and lying flat; consider an epidural blood patch if severe and persistent beyond 48 h.
Traumatic tap – if >10 × 10⁶ RBC/µL, correct for blood contamination before interpreting glucose and protein; repeat LP if needed.
Seizure after LP – give benzodiazepine, then load with antiepileptic (e.g., levetiracetam) and monitor EEG if available.
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, worsening consciousness) after LP – stop further CSF removal, raise head of bed, start hyperosmolar therapy, and arrange urgent neuro‑imaging.
Nosocomial infection at puncture site – apply sterile dressing, start empiric coverage if cellulitis develops, and consider removal of any indwelling catheter.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, CSF interpretation and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV – higher likelihood of cryptococcal, TB and fungal meningitis; CSF may show low glucose and lymphocytic predominance; add amphotericin B plus flucytosine for cryptococcus.
Malnutrition – impaired immunity leads to atypical bacterial pathogens; monitor for hypoglycaemia after LP and give dextrose if glucose <40 mg/dL.
Pregnancy – avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., chloramphenicol); use ceftriaxone and ampicillin; consider fetal monitoring if maternal sepsis.
Diabetes – steroids and infection raise glucose; check capillary glucose every 4 h and adjust insulin accordingly.
Renal failure – dose‑adjust vancomycin and aminoglycosides; prefer cefotaxime over ceftriaxone if bilirubin is high.
Liver failure – avoid high‑dose paracetamol for headache; use acetaminophen sparingly and monitor transaminases.

sections.p: Tailoring the lumbar puncture approach and management to vulnerable populations improves outcomes in low‑resource settings.
b: Children – use atraumatic 22‑25 G needle, position in lateral decubitus with hips flexed; normal CSF pressure 10‑20 cm H₂O; avoid excessive CSF removal to prevent herniation.
Elderly – higher risk of spinal stenosis; consider ultrasound guidance; be vigilant for subdural haematoma after traumatic tap.
People with HIV – perform India‑ink stain or cryptococcal antigen test on CSF; start antifungal therapy early; monitor for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome if ART is started.
Low‑resource hospitals – if Gram stain unavailable, rely on CSF appearance, cell count and protein; use bedside rapid antigen tests for cryptococcus and TB (e.g., lateral flow assay).
Pregnant women – perform LP only after ruling out contraindications; give ceftriaxone plus ampicillin; avoid radiographic imaging unless absolutely necessary.

facts: Normal opening CSF pressure in children: 10‑20 cm H₂O (≈7‑15 mmHg).
CSF protein normal in children: 15‑45 mg/dL.
CSF glucose normal: 2/3 of simultaneous serum glucose; >45 mg/dL in most children.
Bacterial meningitis CSF: neutrophils >1000/µL, protein >100 mg/dL, glucose <40 mg/dL or <0.4 serum.
Viral meningitis CSF: lymphocytes 10‑500/µL, protein <100 mg/dL, glucose normal.
TB meningitis CSF: lymphocytes 100‑500/µL, protein 100‑500 mg/dL, glucose <45 mg/dL or <0.5 serum.
Post‑LP headache risk factors: age <30, female, multiple attempts, large gauge needle.
Contraindication: papilledema or focal neuro deficit indicating raised ICP without prior CT.
Rapid cryptococcal test: lateral flow assay on CSF, positive if visible test line.
Dexamethasone dose for bacterial meningitis: given before or with first antibiotic dose.

vivas.q: Which ligament is pierced immediately before the dura mater during a lumbar puncture?
vivas.a: The ligamentum flavum lies just superficial to the dura mater.

vivas.q: What is the normal range of lumbar CSF opening pressure in children?
Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated as the first step when a CT shows obstructed ventricles?
vivas.a: Obstructed ventricles indicate raised intracranial pressure; LP could cause brain herniation.

vivas.q: An elderly patient with normal‑pressure hydrocephalus has enlarged ventricles but normal CSF pressure. How is this physiologically classified?
vivas.a: It is classified as communicating hydrocephalus with normal opening pressure.

vivas.q: Which CSF finding 12 h after a thunderclap headache confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage?
vivas.a: Xanthochromia (yellow discoloration) of the supernatant after centrifugation.

vivas.q: A patient with SAH develops premature ventricular complexes and bradycardia within 48 h. What is the likely cause?
vivas.a: Neurogenic cardiac dysfunction due to catecholamine surge from subarachnoid blood.

vivas.q: Why should an experienced proceduralist perform the first LP in a child with suspected ALL?
vivas.a: Because traumatic taps can contaminate CSF, affect cytology, and increase infection risk; expertise reduces these errors.

vivas.q: When is a lumbar puncture strictly indicated in an infant or child with fever and a seizure?
vivas.a: If the child is <12 months, immunocompromised, or has meningeal signs, focal neurologic deficit, or altered consciousness.

vivas.q: Outline the AAP recommendations for LP in a child with febrile seizure.
vivas.a: LP is recommended for children <12 months, or >12 months with immunodeficiency, focal signs, or prolonged seizure; otherwise may be deferred.

vivas.q: What bedside sign helps differentiate meningitis from viral encephalitis?
vivas.a: Neck stiffness with positive Brudzinski or Kernig sign is more typical of meningitis; encephalitis often lacks meningeal irritation.

vivas.q: How do you interpret a CSF glucose of 55 mg/dL when serum glucose is 120 mg/dL?
vivas.a: CSF glucose is ~45% of serum, within normal range; does not suggest bacterial meningitis.

vivas.q: Why is dexamethasone added to empirical therapy for bacterial meningitis?
vivas.a: It reduces inflammatory cytokine release, decreasing neurologic complications, especially in pneumococcal meningitis.

vivas.q: In a low‑resource setting without PCR, how is tuberculous meningitis diagnosed?
vivas.a: Rely on CSF pattern (lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose), acid‑fast stain, and clinical picture; start empiric anti‑TB therapy.

vivas.q: What is the first step if a child with suspected meningitis has a papilledema on exam?
vivas.a: Obtain an urgent CT scan before LP to rule out mass effect; defer LP until imaging is clear.

vivas.q: How can you reduce the risk of post‑LP headache in children?
vivas.a: Use a small‑gauge (≤22G) atraumatic needle, limit attempts, keep the patient supine for 1‑2 h, and ensure adequate hydration.

vivas.q: What CSF finding distinguishes cryptococcal meningitis in an HIV patient?
vivas.a: Positive cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay; India ink may show encapsulated yeasts.

vivas.q: When CSF Gram stain is negative but bacterial meningitis is still suspected, what is the next step?
vivas.a: Start empirical antibiotics promptly; send CSF for culture and consider PCR if available.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a traumatic tap with >500 RBC/µL?
vivas.a: It may obscure xanthochromia; correct for blood by subtracting 1 RBC = 1 µg/dL bilirubin; repeat LP if needed.

mcqs.q: A 6‑month‑old infant presents with fever, irritability and bulging fontanelle. CSF shows clear fluid, protein 30 mg/dL, glucose 65 mg/dL, 2 lymphocytes. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform urgent CT before any treatment.
Observe and repeat LP in 24 h.
Start empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis.
mcqs.e: Normal CSF values in an infant are reassuring; however, clinical suspicion remains high, so start antibiotics immediately.

mcqs.q: Which of the following CSF patterns is most typical for tuberculous meningitis?
mcqs.e: TB meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old with sudden thunderclap headache undergoes LP 12 h later. CSF is clear but spectrophotometry shows a yellow supernatant. What does this indicate?
Which bedside maneuver is most sensitive for detecting meningeal irritation in children?
mcqs.e: Brudzinski sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion) is more sensitive in children.

mcqs.q: In a child with suspected meningitis and papilledema, the safest immediate action is:
o: Proceed with LP using a smaller needle.
Obtain urgent CT scan before LP.
mcqs.e: Papilledema suggests raised ICP; CT is required before LP.

mcqs.q: Which rapid test is most useful for diagnosing cryptococcal meningitis in an HIV‑positive patient?
mcqs.e: The cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay is highly sensitive and quick.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old with normal‑pressure hydrocephalus has an opening pressure of 12 cm H₂O. How is this condition classified?
mcqs.e: Normal‑pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating type with normal opening pressure.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to lumbar puncture?
o: Local skin infection over insertion site.
mcqs.e: Hypertension alone is not a contraindication; coagulopathy, infection, and raised ICP are.

cases.v: A 2‑year‑old boy is brought from a rural clinic with 2 days of fever, vomiting, and a bulging anterior fontanelle. He is irritable, has a positive Brudzinski sign, and no focal deficits. CSF obtained shows clear fluid, protein 90 mg/dL, glucose 40 mg/dL (serum 100 mg/dL), 150 neutrophils/µL.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What immediate management steps should be taken?
qs.a: Give dexamethasone and start empirical IV ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; monitor vitals, glucose, electrolytes.

qs.q: If the child had a visible papilledema on exam, how would your approach change?
qs.a: Obtain an urgent CT scan before LP; defer LP until imaging excludes mass effect.

cases.v: A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman (CD4 80) presents with headache, low‑grade fever, and progressive confusion. LP shows clear fluid, protein 120 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 110 mg/dL), 30 lymphocytes/µL, and a positive cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay.

qs.q: What is the first‑line treatment regimen?
qs.a: Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, followed by fluconazole consolidation.

qs.q: Which CSF finding helps differentiate this from TB meningitis?
qs.a: Positive cryptococcal antigen; TB meningitis would show higher lymphocyte count and often negative antigen.

mistakes: Confusing the ligamentum flavum with the interspinous ligament as the last structure before dura.
Using the adult normal CSF pressure range (70‑180 mmH₂O) for children, leading to misinterpretation.
Performing LP without prior CT when papilledema or focal deficits are present, risking herniation.
Relying on a single negative Gram stain to rule out bacterial meningitis; antibiotics must be started empirically.
Failing to correct CSF glucose for serum glucose, causing false low‑glucose interpretation.
Using large‑bore cutting needles, increasing post‑LP headache rates.
Neglecting to consider HIV‑related opportunistic infections when CSF glucose is low but neutrophils are not dominant.
Assuming normal CSF protein rules out TB meningitis; TB can have modestly elevated protein.
